texts.facts: 3. The brief facts of the case is that on 01.11.1989, the Food Inspector inspected the shop of the Raj Kumar Mittal vs The State Of Jharkhand on 23 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/195839097/ 1 petitioner no.1 and purchased three packets of salt from the petitioner no.2 who was attending the business of the shop of the petitioner no.1. The license of the inspected shop is in the name of the petitioner no.1. The three packets of salt were sealed. Notice under Form -VI was given to the petitioner no.2 who signed the notice and the paper slips were affixed on the packets and the signatures of the petitioner no.2 were obtained on the paper slips. The Food Inspector also prepared a memorandum and sent the memo along with one part of sample to Public Analyst and remaining part to the Local Health Authority. The sample was tested and it was reported that the salt was both adulterated and misbranded. The petitioners pleaded not guilty to the charges and claimed to be tried. During the trial, three witnesses were examined by the prosecution and the documents which were proved have been marked Exhibit -1 to 7. 4. Out of the three prosecution witnesses, P.W.3 was tendered for cross-examination only. P.W.1 -Ashok Kumar Singh is the informant of the case. He is the Food Inspector. He has supported the case of the prosecution. He has inter alia stated that the Form -VI was prepared along with one part of sample. The same was sent to Public Analyst and rest two parts of the sample were sent to the Local Health Authority. The report of the Public Analyst stated that the salt was both misbranded and adulterated. The report of the Public Analyst has been marked Exhibit -4. The seized sample salt was also sent to the Central Food Laboratory and the report of the Central Food Laboratory has been marked Exhibit -7. In his cross-examination, he has stated that though the prosecution report which is in printed form stated that the seized sample of the salt was sealed in a bottle, but the seized sample salt was sealed in the packet itself. Since the packet was not labeled, the P.W.1 suspected it to be adulterated. The packet also did not state the batch code number. The P.W.1 further stated that he endeavoured to call local persons as witnesses but no one became ready to be the witness of seizure. The P.W.1 also stated that the iodized salt should contain 15 ppm of iodine and as per the Act; selling salt without iodine is an offence. 5. P.W.2 -Ram Prasad Singh accompanied the P.W.1 on the date of occurrence to the shop of the petitioners. He has also supported the case of the prosecution. He has also stated that the salt was not sealed in bottle.
texts.arguments: 7. Mr. J.K. Pasari, the learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the learned court below could not properly appreciate the evidence in the record in their right perspective. So far as the allegation of misbranding is concerned, it is submitted by Mr. Pasari that Rule 32 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 has been declared ultra vires the rule making power, by the Hon'ble Raj Kumar Mittal vs The State Of Jharkhand on 23 September, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/195839097/ 2 Supreme Court of India in the case of Dwarka Nath v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi, reported in (1971) 2 SCC 314, hence the court below ought not have convicted and sentenced the petitioners for misbranding. It is next submitted by Mr. Pasari that as per Rule A.15.01 of the Appendix -B of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 prepared in terms of Rule 5 thereof contains the definition and standards quality for distribution channel including retail level iodized salt is not supposed to contain less than 15 parts per million (ppm) on dry-wet basis. Relying upon the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Vijendra Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, reported in (2020) 15 SCC 763, para -16 to 18 of which reads as under:- "16. 17. In this regard, it is apposite to take note of the decision rendered by this Court in K. Harikumar v. Punaloor Municipality [K. Harikumar v. Punaloor Municipality, 1995 Supp (3) SCC 405 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 933] relied upon by the learned counsel for the appellant, wherein while considering the provisions of the 1954 Act with regard to the sample of curd which was the subject-matter therein, it was held that in order to attain homogeneity in curd, stirring and churning may become necessary for the ingredients of the milk solid non-fat and milk solid fat getting consistency in order to determine the percentage in their completeness. 18. In that background, in the instant case, as already noticed the Public Analyst had opined that the milk sample was deficient by 12% in milk fat and 27% in non-fatty solids. Manner of sending samples for analysis. - Samples of food for the purpose of analysis shall be taken in clean dry bottles or jars or in other suitable containers which shall be closed sufficiently tight to prevent leakage, evaporation, or in the case of dry substance, entrance of moisture and shall be carefully sealed." and which mandates that the samples of food for the purpose of analysis shall be kept in clean dry bottles or jars or in other suitable containers which shall be closed sufficiently tight to prevent leakage, evaporation or in case of dry substance, entrance of moisture and shall be carefully sealed; has not been complied with, as both the material witnesses examined by the prosecution have categorically stated that the sample was kept in a plastic packet and not in bottle as envisaged in law and the P.W.2 has categorically stated that the sample was not sealed, certainly are grounds sufficient enough to given benefit of doubt to the petitioners. 8. It is further submitted by Mr. Pasari that a valuable right of the petitioners of giving them the opportunity of getting the second sample examined by the Central Food Laboratory was reduced to a mere formality as it is evident that the sample was sent after five years since the date of collection of sample as the same was sent on 09.09.1994 and as is evident from the order dated 16.05.1994 of the order sheet of the trial court that the second sample of the case was destroyed by rats. 9. The learned Spl. P.P. on the other hand defended the impugned judgment and submitted that the evidence in the record is sufficient to establish the charge for the offence punishable under Section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 both the courts below having rightly held the petitioners guilty for the said offence and the sentence imposed being minimum , this revision petition being without any merit be dismissed. It is a settled principle of law that the provisions of Section 13 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 is mandatory, as has been held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of State of Orissa Vs. Gouranga Sahu, reported in AIR 2004 SC 1233. 11.
